title: Spaghetti Bolognese
subtitle: Slow-cooked meat ragù from Bologna
excerpt: A slow-cooked ragù of beef and pork mince with wine, tomato, and milk, tossed with spaghetti and served with Parmesan. The Italian original is richer and slower than most British versions.

recipe.sourceNotes: Ragù alla Bolognese originates from Bologna in Emilia-Romagna and is one of the most famous pasta sauces in the world. The registered recipe of the Italian Academy of Cuisine (1982) calls for beef, pork belly, onion, carrot, celery, tomato paste, whole milk, dry white wine, and optional chicken livers. The slow-cooked, meat-heavy sauce is quite different from the tomato-heavy British interpretation commonly known as 'spag bol'. The key techniques are: browning the meat properly, adding liquid in stages, and a long, slow simmer with the lid off for the last hour to concentrate the flavour.

recipeTools.notes: Wide and heavy-based for the ragù.

content.text: The traditional Bolognese uses much less tomato than most people expect: it is a meat sauce with a little tomato, not a tomato sauce with meat. The milk added partway through tenderises the meat and adds richness. The ragù needs a minimum of 2 hours at the lowest possible simmer: 3 to 4 hours is better. The sauce should finish with most of the liquid evaporated, the meat very soft, and the colour a deep, dark brown.
Heat the oil in a wide, heavy pan over medium heat. Fry the pancetta for 3 minutes. Add the onion, carrot, and celery. Cook for 10 minutes until soft. Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute.

Increase the heat. Add the beef and pork mince in batches. Brown well, breaking up any clumps. This takes 10 to 12 minutes. Add the tomato puree and cook for 2 minutes. Pour in the wine and bubble until mostly evaporated.

Add the tinned tomatoes, bay leaves, and milk. Season. Bring to a gentle simmer. Cook uncovered on the lowest heat for at least 2 hours, stirring occasionally, until the sauce is very thick, dark, and reduced. Add a splash of water if it looks dry. Taste and adjust seasoning.

Cook the spaghetti in well-salted boiling water until al dente. Reserve a mug of pasta water. Drain. Toss the spaghetti with the ragù, adding a splash of pasta water to loosen if needed. Serve with grated Parmesan.
